h1: The 6 Best Kensington Laptop Locks of 2026, Ranked & Reviewed
metaTitle: Best Kensington Laptop Locks: Ranked & Reviewed
metaDescription: Ranked and reviewed by Primea: six Kensington laptop locks compared on slot type, combination or key, cable length and warranty so the lock fits your laptop.
summary: The Kensington Universal 3-in-1 2.0 (K63394WW) is the best laptop lock, with one tip that fits Standard, Nano and Wedge slots. The older 3-in-1 uses swappable tips and adds code recovery. Specialist locks cover Standard-only, Nano and Dell Wedge slots, including one keyed model.
intro: The first mistake with a laptop lock is buying one that does not fit. Kensington sells three slot formats, Standard T-Bar, Nano and the Dell Wedge, and a lock made for one will not seat in another, however hard you push. A lock that cannot seat protects nothing, and the mismatch only shows once the lock is in your hand.

We ranked six Kensington locks on the listing data for slot type, key or combination, cable length and support. The order favors locks that work across more laptops, then the specialist models. A cable lock also deters opportunists rather than determined thieves, which is worth remembering when you choose what to anchor it to.

products.name: Kensington Universal 3-in-1 2.0 Combination Laptop Lock, K63394WW
products.verdict: One tip that fits the three common slot types.
products.description:
The K63394WW has one tip that fits Standard, Nano and N17 Wedge slots, a 360-degree rotatable head and a 6 foot cut-resistant cable, with a resettable 4-digit combination, in the $25 to $50 bracket. One tip fitting all three slots removes the biggest risk in this category. The rotatable head also matters: a lock that can turn to any angle copes with tight ports and awkward desk layouts.

It ranks first because it fits every common slot and rotates to any angle. The older 3-in-1 uses swappable tips that can be lost, and the specialist locks fit only one format each.

Buy it if you own several laptops or may change. The caveats are the $25 to $50 price, above the cheapest lock here, and a four-digit combination you can forget. Write the code down somewhere safe.
products.skipIf: You only need one slot type.

products.name: Kensington Universal 3-in-1 Combination Laptop Lock, K62316WW
products.verdict: Swappable Standard, Nano and Wedge tips on one cable.
products.description:
The K62316WW has interchangeable Standard, Nano and Wedge tips, with the spares tethered so they do not get lost, a 6 foot cut-resistant cable and Register and Retrieve code recovery, in the $25 to $50 bracket. Code recovery is the standout. If you forget the combination, the online service can retrieve it, which turns a locked and useless cable into a minor inconvenience.

It ranks second because the 2.0 version uses a single tip and avoids swapping altogether. Swapping tips takes a minute and is easy to get wrong, though the tethers keep the spares from vanishing.

Choose it if recovering a forgotten code matters, such as for a shared office pool. Skip it if you dislike swapping tips. Both 3-in-1 models cost the same, so pick on convenience versus recovery.
products.idealFor: People who might forget a code.

products.name: Kensington Combination Cable T-Bar Standard Lock for Laptops, K64673AM
products.description:
The K64673AM fits the standard T-Bar slot only, not the Dell and Alienware Wedge. It has a resettable 4-wheel code with 10,000 combinations and a 6 foot cut-resistant carbon steel cable, independently torque and pull tested, in the $25 to $50 bracket. Ten thousand combinations means a thief cannot guess the code quickly, and independent testing lends credibility to the strength claims.

It ranks third because it fits one slot type only. It is a proven simple design, and the carbon steel cable is independently tested for torque and pull.

Buy it for a laptop with a standard slot. The caveats are the single-slot limit and no code recovery, so choose a code you will remember. A Nano or Wedge laptop port rejects it, so check the shape first.
products.idealFor: Laptops with a standard T-Bar slot.
products.skipIf: Your laptop has a Nano or Wedge slot.

products.name: Kensington NanoSaver Combination Laptop Lock, K60603WW
products.verdict: A slim head for Nano slots.
products.description:
The K60603WW fits the Nano slot on select HP, Lenovo and Asus models and some docking stations, with a slim head that keeps the laptop flat and avoids blocking ports, and Register and Retrieve online code recovery, in the $25 to $50 bracket. Thin laptops have tight port clusters, and a bulky lock head can cover the neighboring port.

It ranks fourth because it fits Nano slots only, and only select models. The slim head and code recovery are real strengths, and it is the only lock here named for docking stations.

Choose it if your laptop has a Nano slot. Check your model against the supported list before buying, because select models means not all. Skip it if the laptop uses a different slot, since the universal 2.0 fits all three at the same bracket.
products.skipIf: Your laptop has a different slot.

products.name: Kensington N17 Dell Laptop Combination Lock, K68008WW
products.verdict: The Wedge-slot lock for Dell and Alienware.
products.description:
The K68008WW fits the Dell and Alienware Wedge slot only. It uses a resettable 4-wheel code with 10,000 combinations and a 6 foot cut-resistant cable, independently torque and pull tested, and costs under $25. It is the cheapest lock here.

It ranks fifth because it works with one slot type. The price is the draw: a Dell office could equip many desks for little. Strength and combination count match the T-Bar model.

Buy it for a Dell laptop with a Wedge slot. The caveat is that it is not universal, so a replacement laptop from another brand makes the lock useless. Skip it if you own other brands, and compare it with the keyed N17 below if your office prefers keys.

products.name: Kensington N17 Dell Laptop Lock, Keyed, K64440WW
products.verdict: A keyed Wedge lock with a pivoting head.
products.description:
The K64440WW is keyed with a 5mm anti-pick pin system for the Dell and Alienware Wedge slot, in the $25 to $50 bracket. Its pivot-and-rotate head keeps its hold when the cable moves, and it is TAA compliant and independently tested for torque, pull and corrosion. An anti-pick system resists casual picking.

It ranks last because it uses a key instead of a code, so the key can be lost, and it fits Wedge only. The TAA compliance suits some offices that need it for purchasing rules.

Pick it for an office that wants keys and has Dell hardware. The caveat is the key: store a spare in a safe place, because a lost key leaves the laptop tethered. Skip it if you hate carrying keys.

whatMatters.detail: A laptop's lock slot comes in different shapes. Standard T-Bar, Nano and the Dell Wedge are not interchangeable. Look at the slot on your laptop, or find it in the specs, before ordering. If you are unsure, the Universal 3-in-1 2.0 fits all three, which removes the guess and any risk of a wrong purchase. Measure nothing, just match the shape.

Combination locks have no key to lose but can be forgotten. Keyed locks need a spare key. Choose based on how many people share the laptop and who manages the codes or keys. A forgotten code or a lost key is a bigger problem than the lock type. A single owner suits a combination with recovery, while a managed office may prefer keys held by IT.

A 6 foot cable gives enough reach to loop around a table leg. Check that the object you tether to is fixed and sturdy, because a lock is only as strong as its anchor, and a light chair or a movable desk defeats it. All six locks here list 6 feet, so differences come from the head and tip.

A rotatable or pivoting head holds better when the cable moves, and a slim head avoids blocking ports. These are named in the listing. The K63394WW rotates 360 degrees, the K64440WW pivots and the K60603WW is slim, so pick the one that fits your port layout and desk position. A lock head that blocks a neighboring port is an everyday irritation, and a stiff head can strain the slot.

Register and Retrieve lets you recover a forgotten code. It is useful for combination locks, especially for shared laptops. The listing names the service, and the K62316WW and K60603WW include it. Without it, a forgotten code means cutting the cable, so register the lock when you buy and store the confirmation email. Keep the registration details separate from the laptop bag so a thief cannot use them.

faq.q: How do I know my laptop's slot type?
faq.a: Look at the slot on the laptop. Standard, Nano and Wedge shapes differ, and the laptop's spec page usually names the slot too. If unsure, the Universal 3-in-1 2.0 fits all three, so you avoid a wrong purchase, and it will keep working if you change laptops later.

faq.q: Can a lock stop all theft?
faq.a: No. A cable lock deters opportunists but a determined thief can cut or break it. Use it as a deterrent and keep valuables out of sight as well, because a visible laptop attracts attention first.

faq.q: Is the 2.0 worth it over the original 3-in-1?
faq.a: If you dislike swapping tips, yes. If you want online code recovery, the original lists it, and the 2.0 does not name the service. Pick on convenience or recovery, because both lock to the same slot types for the same bracket.

faq.q: How do I set the combination?
faq.a: Follow the instructions in the package, and set the code before you attach the cable. Write the code down in a safe place, and test the lock before you rely on it, spinning the wheels fully so the new code sticks. The 4-wheel models allow 10,000 combinations.

faq.q: What do I attach the cable to?
faq.a: A fixed object such as a heavy table leg or a built-in anchor. A light chair or desk that can be lifted defeats the six foot cable, so check what you attach to.

faq.q: Can I use one on a docking station?
faq.a: The NanoSaver lists some docking stations. Check your dock's slot type, and confirm that it matches the lock before ordering a Nano or Wedge model. Many docks have no slot at all.

finalTake: Buy the Universal 3-in-1 2.0 if you own several laptops or may change brands. Take the older 3-in-1 for code recovery, and a specialist lock only if you know your slot type. Dell and Alienware owners can save money with the N17 locks. Read the slot on your laptop first.
